title: SHE HAD EVERYTHING—AND STILL BETRAYED THE ONE WHO LOVED HER
paragraphs: SHE HAD EVERYTHING—AND STILL BETRAYED THE ONE WHO LOVED HER
Ezekiel 16 uses the shocking language of marriage, adultery, and prostitution to expose Jerusalem’s betrayal—but buried beneath the scandal is a truth about grace that may expose something in us too.
There are chapters of the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you uncomfortable enough to wonder why God allowed them to remain in Scripture.
Ezekiel 16 is one of those chapters.
It is graphic.
Painful.
Deliberately humiliating.
It speaks of nakedness, marriage, adultery, prostitution, blood, lovers, betrayal, judgment, and shame.
Read quickly, and it can sound almost unbearably severe.
But read carefully…
and something devastating begins to emerge.
This chapter is not primarily a story about sex.
It is a story about covenant betrayal.
And before you distance yourself from Jerusalem and say, “I would never do what she did,” you may want to keep reading.
Because Ezekiel 16 eventually forces a much more frightening question:
What if spiritual adultery does not always look like leaving God?
What if sometimes it looks like keeping His name while quietly giving your heart to something else?
Jerusalem’s story begins in a place nobody would expect.
Not with prostitution.
Not with rebellion.
Not even with judgment.
It begins with abandonment.
God commands Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with her abominations, and then He describes the city through the imagery of an unwanted newborn.
No one cared for her.
No one cleaned her.
No one wrapped her.
No one showed compassion.
She was pictured as discarded in a field.
Then God passed by.
And God said:
Live.
That is where the story begins.
Grace found her before beauty did.
Grace found her before status did.
Grace found her before she had anything with which to repay God.
Later, the imagery changes.
Jerusalem matures, and God describes entering into covenant with her.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:8 is striking:
וָאֶשָּׁבַע לָךְ וָאָבוֹא בִבְרִית אֹתָךְ
Va’eshava lakh, va’avo bivrit otakh.
In context: God swore an oath to her and entered into a בְּרִית — berit, a covenant, with her.
Then comes the breathtaking declaration:
וַתִּהְיִי לִי — vattihyi li
“You became Mine.”
Not because Jerusalem rescued herself.
God found her.
God gave her life.
God covered her.
God entered covenant with her.
God washed her.
God clothed her.
God adorned her.
God provided for her.
The abandoned became beloved.
The discarded became beautiful.
The one lying helpless became a bride.
And that is precisely what makes what happens next so horrifying.
Because the tragedy of Ezekiel 16 is not merely that Jerusalem sinned.
It is that she took the gifts of the One who loved her…
and used those gifts to betray Him.
God says Jerusalem became confident in her beauty.
Then Ezekiel uses a Hebrew verb that keeps haunting the chapter:
זנה — zanah.
It carries the idea of engaging in prostitution or harlotry.
Ezekiel 16 repeatedly employs sexual infidelity as a prophetic metaphor for Jerusalem’s covenant unfaithfulness.
This is not permission to demean women who have suffered exploitation, nor is Ezekiel giving human beings permission to weaponize sexual shame against sinners.
The target of the prophetic accusation is Jerusalem herself, personified as an unfaithful covenant partner.
The metaphor is intentionally shocking because covenant betrayal is serious.
Jerusalem had received gifts from God and redirected them toward idols.
She sought other “lovers.”
She pursued foreign powers.
She participated in idolatry.
And the chapter descends into something even darker: God accuses Jerusalem of sacrificing children.
This was not a harmless spiritual phase.
This was rebellion consuming human lives.
But there is something about the metaphor that becomes almost unbearable.
Ordinarily, Ezekiel observes, a prostitute receives payment.
Jerusalem’s behavior is portrayed as the reverse.
She gives gifts to her lovers.
She pays them.
Think about that.
She is not merely being tempted away.
She is financing her own betrayal.
She is spending what God gave her to pursue what cannot replace God.
And suddenly Ezekiel 16 stops feeling ancient.
Because we know something about doing that.
God gives us time…
and we can spend it avoiding Him.
God gives us influence…
and we can use it to glorify ourselves.
God gives us money…
and we can make money our master.
God gives us relationships…
and we can demand from people the security only God can ultimately provide.
God gives us bodies…
and we can turn desire into a ruler.
God gives us abilities…
and we can become addicted to applause.
God gives us technology…
and we can allow it to fill our minds with things that slowly deaden our hunger for holiness.
God gives us blessings…
and sometimes the blessing becomes more precious to us than the Blesser.
That is when Ezekiel 16 becomes personal.
Because an idol does not have to be a statue.
An idol can be anything we allow to occupy the place of trust, worship, identity, obedience, or ultimate devotion that belongs to God.
Success can become a lover.
Approval can become a lover.
Money can become a lover.
Pornography can become a lover.
Resentment can become a lover.
Attention can become a lover.
A relationship can become a lover.
Even ministry can become one if we begin loving the platform more than the Christ we claim to proclaim.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual affairs are the ones nobody sees.
You can still attend church.
Still quote Scripture.
Still post Christian content.
Still sing worship songs.
Still say “God is good.”
And somewhere beneath all of it, your heart can be whispering:
Jesus, You can have everything except this.
That sentence should frighten us.
Because Jesus is not looking for a religious arrangement in which we occasionally visit Him while our deepest allegiance belongs elsewhere.
He is Lord.
And Ezekiel 16 exposes the insanity of sin:
We abandon living water and then wonder why our souls remain thirsty.
We chase approval and remain insecure.
We chase pleasure and discover that appetite grows faster than satisfaction.
We chase control and become increasingly afraid.
We chase money and discover there is always another number.
We chase attention and discover applause cannot love us.
Jerusalem kept chasing lovers.
And she was not satisfied.
Neither are we.
Sin makes enormous promises.
Then sends an invoice.
Eventually the lovers Jerusalem pursued could not save her from judgment.
That is another truth we desperately need.
Whatever replaces God eventually fails under the weight of being God.
Your spouse cannot carry that weight.
Your children cannot carry it.
Your career cannot carry it.
Your pastor cannot carry it.
Your followers cannot carry it.
Money cannot carry it.
Pleasure cannot carry it.
You were created for God.
And there is another uncomfortable layer here.
Sometimes we think grace means God does not care very much about our betrayal.
Ezekiel 16 destroys that idea.
God's judgment in this chapter is severe precisely because covenant rebellion is not trivial.
Biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace becomes astonishing because sin does matter.
God is holy.
Evil matters.
Idolatry matters.
Injustice matters.
The shedding of innocent blood matters.
Our rebellion matters.
And yet Ezekiel 16 does not finish where you might expect.
After exposure…
after betrayal…
after judgment…
after shame…
God speaks about covenant again.
Near the end of the chapter, He promises to remember His covenant and speaks of establishing an everlasting covenant.
That does not erase the judgment.
It reveals something extraordinary about God.
Human unfaithfulness does not transform God into an unfaithful God.
And now the entire biblical story begins pulling us forward.
Because Jerusalem's problem was not merely political.
Humanity's deepest problem is not merely behavioral.
We need more than improved habits.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need cleansing.
We need a new heart.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel announces His name.
Jesus Christ.
The New Testament brings covenant and bride imagery to its breathtaking fulfillment in Christ.
Jesus does not come searching for people who can prove they never betrayed God.
He comes to save sinners.
At the cross, He does not call evil good.
He bears judgment.
He deals with sin at immeasurable cost.
The scandal of grace is not that God shrugged at our rebellion.
The scandal is that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the One we betrayed becomes the only One capable of bringing us home.
That is why repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
Repentance is turning.
Coming out of hiding.
Dropping the idols.
Ending the affair with sin.
Returning to God through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been using God's gifts while ignoring God.
Maybe nobody knows what owns you when the room gets quiet.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your worship playlist.
Maybe bitterness has lived inside you so long that you stopped calling it bitterness.
Maybe success became your identity.
Maybe you love being seen as Christian more than you love Christ.
Maybe you have repeatedly promised God, “Never again,” only to find yourself crawling back to the same thing.
And perhaps shame has convinced you that after everything you have done, Jesus would never want you.
Then remember where Ezekiel 16 began.
In the field.
Abandoned.
Covered in blood.
Unable to rescue herself.
And God said:
Live.
Grace began before Jerusalem had anything impressive to offer.
And for the Christian, grace reaches its blazing center at a bloodstained cross.
You do not clean yourself enough to make Christ willing to save you.
You come to Christ because you cannot save yourself.
You confess.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender.
And Jesus does what our idols never could.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He gives life.
He begins transforming the very heart that wandered from Him.
This is why your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is mighty to save.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming rebellion as freedom.
Not by telling us we were secretly righteous all along.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's story through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
He takes what sin shattered and begins restoration.
He takes the guilty and justifies those who come to Him by faith.
He takes the spiritually dead and gives life.
He takes wanderers and brings them home.
He takes people hiding in shame and teaches them to walk in the light.
So do not finish this article by thinking only about Jerusalem.
Ask the harder question.
Who—or what—has been receiving the devotion that belongs to Jesus?
Do not answer publicly if doing so would expose something unsafe or deeply private.
But answer God.
Tell Him the truth.
No performance.
No religious language designed to impress anybody.
Just truth.
“Jesus, I have wandered.”
“Jesus, I have loved things more than You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, teach me to want You again.”
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer reads at midnight and realizes they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to prove that you love God.
But because when believers freely support Gospel-centered work, they help that work continue reaching people with Scripture and the message of Jesus Christ.
And there is more waiting for those serious about going deeper.

If this ministry has been feeding your faith, sharpening your convictions, helping you understand Scripture, or pointing you back toward Jesus, consider becoming part of the community that helps keep this Gospel work moving.
Invite someone to follow with you.
And do not underestimate what God can do when biblical truth reaches one person at exactly the moment their heart is finally ready to hear it.
Because Ezekiel 16 leaves us with a truth far bigger than Jerusalem's scandal.
The God who exposes sin is also the God who calls sinners to return.
And when you finally stop running, you may discover that the story you thought ended in shame was standing at the doorway of grace.
The idol knows how to take your gifts. Jesus knows how to resurrect your story.
